definition: Systematic and unfair skew in a model's predictions or behavior, often reflecting imbalances or prejudices present in its training data.
details: Bias in ML systems can perpetuate or amplify societal inequities, making bias detection, measurement, and mitigation an important part of responsible model development and evaluation.

explainer.lead: Bias in machine learning is a systematic, unfair tilt in what a model predicts or how it behaves. It matters because a model can repeat or strengthen existing inequities even when its overall accuracy looks good.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a judge who has mostly seen examples that favor one team and then keeps favoring that team without good reason. A model can do something similar when its training examples are unbalanced or prejudiced. People check for this pattern and try to correct it so the model treats people more fairly.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, teams look for systematic differences in predictions or errors across relevant groups during development and evaluation, then investigate whether training-data imbalances or prejudices could explain them. Mitigation belongs alongside detection and measurement rather than being treated as a one-time fix. A high aggregate score can hide group-specific harm, and a measured disparity needs context before it is labeled unfair.
tiers.paperLevel: A common measurement starting point is a group disparity such as Δ = E[Ŷ | G=g] − E[Ŷ | G=h], with analogous gaps defined for error rates; the entry’s notion of bias requires the skew to be systematic and unfair, not merely nonzero. Bias may reflect imbalances or prejudices in training data and can perpetuate or amplify societal inequities. A disparity statistic alone does not establish unfairness, and reducing one measured gap does not show that bias has been eliminated.

explainer.example: Suppose a loan-screening model is trained on historical approvals in which otherwise similar applicants from one group were approved less often. If it learns that pattern, it may reject qualified applicants from that group at a higher rate; reviewing outcomes by group can expose the gap even when overall accuracy is high.

usedIn.name: Model evaluation
usedIn.detail: Bias detection and measurement help reveal unfair prediction or behavior patterns that aggregate performance can hide.

usedIn.name: Responsible model development
usedIn.detail: Teams use bias mitigation as part of building and reviewing models whose outputs could reinforce societal inequities.

explainer.intuition: A model learns patterns from its examples, so lopsided or prejudiced examples can teach it a lopsided response. The key issue is not an occasional mistake but a repeatable skew that disadvantages people unfairly.
howItWorks: Training data contains imbalances or prejudices connected to past outcomes.
The model learns those patterns along with useful task-related patterns.
Its predictions or behavior then show a systematic, unfair skew.
Evaluation detects and measures the pattern, including disparities hidden by overall performance.
Mitigation and further evaluation aim to reduce the skew and its harmful effects.
explainer.whyItMatters: Biased outputs can perpetuate or amplify societal inequities rather than merely reproduce neutral statistical patterns. Detection, measurement, and mitigation therefore need to be part of responsible development and evaluation.
misconceptions: Bias is not just any prediction error: it is systematic and unfair skew.
High overall accuracy does not show that a model is unbiased.
Adding more data does not automatically help if the new data carries the same imbalances or prejudices.

diagram.caption: Bias can flow from training data into model behavior, while evaluation and mitigation form a feedback loop.
